newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Credit Lyonnais seen posting 1996 profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Credit Lyonnais seen posting 1996 profit.

text.p: Credit Lyonnais, the French bank whose lending excesses nearly triggered its collapse, is expected to report a small profit for 1996 on Thursday but will still need a big dose of public money to prepare it for privatisation.
According to a Reuter poll of 22 analysts, the bank is likely to post a 150 million franc ($26.5 million) profit after limping back into the black last year with a profit of 13 million francs.
"But it could be anything," said a Paris analyst, referring to the state-controlled bank's unpredictable past performance.
Credit Lyonnais accumulated losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994 as a result of an expansion binge that briefly turned it into the largest bank outside Japan.

The government has pledged to present a long-delayed aid package for the bank to the European Union for approval at the end of March. The package, the third in four years, will aim to prepare the bank for sale, but one source said it might not now be submitted until early April.

The government has said it wants to privatise the bank in early 1999. But before that, the bank is expected to need a 10 to 15 billion franc injection of public money to boost solvency ratios and cover losses on asset sales sought by the EU in exchange for sanctioning the aid.

The European Commission, which only two years ago approved a 45 billion franc bailout for the bank, has estimated another 15 to 20 billion francs in state money could be needed to soften the terms of a loan the bank made under the 1995 rescue to finance the spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet.

But those sums pale beside estimates of the total cost of saving the bank. A member of a key parliamentary finance committee said last week the final cost to taxpayers of the rescue was likely to be about 130 billion francs.

Credit Lyonnais is not the only French state-owned institution needing a handout. Last month, the centre-right government said it was poised to pump at least 20 billion francs into insurer GAN to ready it for privatisation.

Analysts say Credit Lyonnais has been slowly getting its act together, cutting operating costs and improving productivity. This, combined with an overall improving banking climate, has been reflected in a doubling of the stock price from last year's record low of 94.55 francs. The shares traded at 900 francs when the bank's fortunes were at their peak in 1990.

"The bank has been putting the focus on the right direction -- on cutting costs and improving the credit quality of the loan book," said analyst John Leonard of Salomon Brothers, who is looking for a 1996 profit of about 170 million francs.
The bank cut its domestic staff to less than 38,000 at mid-1996 from almost 41,000 at the end of 1994. A further 5,000 job cuts are targeted by the end of 1998.

Analysts expect a further rise in the bank's profits for 1997 to about 690 million francs, but most dismiss talk of a big profit improvement. "It's still not close to being a massively profitable bank," said one.

The bank's shares closed 0.21 percent lower at 193.50 francs. The shares have been falling from a near 12-month high reached on March 4 of 237.70 francs in what analysts say may be profit-taking after their steep rise. "I believe these shares have more upside than downside," said one.

But analysts say the ultimate value of the shares -- which they emphasize are a strictly speculative play -- will be determined by the government's privatisation plan which will probably involve a shares-for-cash injection.
The number of shares thus created will be the key determinant of the value of the existing shares, they say. ($ = 5.65 French Francs)
